box.title: Pressure is molecules hitting the walls
box.mini: Each molecule that bounces off a wall gives it a kick of 2 m v. Billions of kicks make a pressure, p = n k T. In a closed box, opposite walls are kicked equally: the pushes cancel.
box.text: A gas is a crowd of molecules flying in straight lines. Each bounce off a wall reverses the molecule's speed across it and gives the wall a kick of 2 m v⊥ (Newton's third law [2]); added up over a square metre and a second, the kicks are the pressure, p = n k T [1]. At sea level about {{hitsSea}} molecules hit each square centimetre every second. In a closed box every wall is kicked as hard as the wall opposite, so a closed box goes nowhere at any pressure. In the animation, 400 balls stand for the molecules and every push is measured from their hits; halfway, every ball is made √2 times faster: each hit is √2 harder and √2 more frequent, the pressure doubles, and the pushes still cancel.
box.verdict: Would refute the picture: a closed box of hot gas that moves by itself, or pressures that do not rise with the temperature.
hole.title: A hole leaves one push without a partner
hole.mini: Cut a hole in the bottom of a box of gas: the top is still hit, the missing piece of bottom is not. The box is pushed up, F = C_F p A, until it is empty.
hole.text: Over a closed box the pushes of the gas add up to zero, F = ∮ p n dA = 0: each piece of wall has an opposite piece. Remove a piece of area A from the bottom and the piece of top opposite it is left unbalanced. The box is pushed upwards by C_F p A, where C_F is ½ for a gas as thin as the animation's, about 1.3 for a dense gas leaving at the speed of sound, and up to about 2 with a well-shaped nozzle in a vacuum [1]. Nothing outside the box takes part. In the animation the box, in empty space, is pushed up as long as gas is left, and the total kick it receives equals the momentum carried off by the balls that left: a balloon let go.
fill.title: How a chamber keeps its pressure next to a vacuum
fill.mini: A vacuum does not suck: a molecule leaves only when its own flight takes it through the throat. The fire makes gas faster than the throat lets it out; the pressure rises until out = in.
fill.text: Empty space has no molecules, so it pulls on nothing; it only fails to push back. How many molecules leave a chamber each second depends on how many are inside, how fast they go and how large the opening is, never on what lies outside. So the gas inside rises until as much leaves as the fire makes, dN/dt = Ṅin − N/τ, and then holds. For a real engine the balance reads p_c = ṁ c*/A_t [1]: the RS-25 holds {{pcBar}} bar in its chamber with {{mdot}} kg/s through a throat {{throatD}} m across [2]. Its throat is choked, the gas passing at the speed of sound, so nothing downstream can change the chamber at all. In the animation the chamber starts empty in empty space, fills, holds, and empties when the fire goes out.
fill.verdict: Would refute it: a chamber whose pressure collapses when the outside is pumped down, at the same fire.
thrust.title: Newton's third law, one hit at a time
thrust.mini: The rocket pushes on its own gas and the gas pushes back on the rocket. The push measured on the walls equals the momentum the jet carries off each second: F = ṁ vₑ + (pₑ − pₐ) Aₑ.
thrust.text: Every hit of a molecule on the top of the chamber pushes the rocket up and the molecule down; the molecule then flies down and out. That is the pair of forces of the third law [1], and the rocket needs nothing else to push on, any more than a gun needs air to recoil. Adding up the hits on every wall gives a push upwards: the top is pushed up harder than the converging walls are pushed down, and the sides cancel. It equals the momentum the jet carries off each second, F = ṁ vₑ + (pₑ − pₐ) Aₑ, where ṁ is the mass leaving each second, vₑ its speed, pₑ and Aₑ the pressure and area at the exit, and pₐ the outside pressure [2]. In the animation the bookkeeping since the start is exact: the rocket's kicks, plus the momentum of the balls inside and of those that left, add up to zero.
thrust.verdict: Would refute the third law: a push on the rocket larger or smaller than the momentum its jet carries off.
air.title: The air does not help a rocket: it holds it back
air.mini: The air pushes on the rocket's skin everywhere except across the nozzle exit, where the jet is: a net push backwards, pₐ Aₑ. Goddard found faster jets in a vacuum in 1916; the RS-25 gives {{gain}} % more thrust there.
air.text: If rockets pushed on the air, they would push harder in thicker air. The thrust equation says the opposite: the air appears only in −pₐ Aₑ, its push on the outside of the rocket wherever the jet is not [1]. The RS-25 gives {{fVac}} kN in a vacuum and {{fSl}} kN at sea level [2]. Goddard fired a steel chamber with a nozzle in air and in a tank pumped down to between {{gHi}} and {{gLo}} of an atmosphere in 1915–1916, and found the gas faster in the vacuum, by up to {{gGain}} % [3]. The New York Times wrote in 1920 that he lacked “something better than a vacuum against which to react”, and printed its correction on 17 July 1969 [4]. In the animation the same rocket, with the same fire, is measured in empty space and in air.
air.verdict: Would vindicate the objection: a rocket that gives less push, or none, once the air is pumped away. Every test since 1916 gives more.
rs25.title: The RS-25: the air's share of the thrust, measured
rs25.mini: {{fVac}} kN in a vacuum, {{fSl}} kN at sea level. The difference, {{diff}} kN, is the sea-level pressure times {{aeDiff}} m², a circle {{dDiff}} m across: the RS-25's nozzle exit is {{exitD}} m.
rs25.text: NASA gives the RS-25, the main engine of the Space Shuttle and of the SLS, at 109 % power: {{fVac}} kN of thrust in a vacuum and {{fSl}} kN at sea level [1], {{gain}} % more where there is no air. The thrust equation says the difference is the air pushing on the exit area, F(vac) − F(sea) = pₐ Aₑ. {{diff}} kN divided by 101.3 kPa is {{aeDiff}} m², a circle {{dDiff}} m across; the nozzle exit is {{exitD}} m across [2]. The specific impulses agree: {{cVac}} km/s of effective exhaust speed in vacuum, {{cSl}} km/s at sea level [2]. Upper stages are hot-fired in vacuum chambers built for the purpose [3].
rs25.verdict: Would refute the account: a sea-level thrust higher than the vacuum thrust, or a difference unrelated to the exit area.
joule.title: “Free expansion does no work”: the rocket is the missing piston
joule.mini: Joule's air spread into an empty vessel and did no work because no wall moved. In a rocket the gas pushes the top of the chamber, and the chamber moves: W = F Δx.
joule.text: In 1845 Joule let compressed air into an evacuated vessel: it spread through both and, since nothing outside moved, did no external work [1]. Work is a force times the distance moved by what is pushed, W = ∫ p dV over the walls that move. A rocket is precisely the moving wall that free expansion lacks: the gas pushes on the top of the chamber with the force F and the chamber moves by Δx, so the gas does the work F Δx on the rocket before leaving. Once outside, the jet does expand freely, and that part pushes nothing. On a fixed test stand the rocket does no work at all and still feels its full thrust: a force needs momentum, not work.
free.title: In empty space the centre of mass never moves
free.mini: A rocket free in space throws its fuel backwards; their common centre of mass stays put, and the rocket speeds up by Δv = u ln(m₀/m₁). For a low orbit at the RS-25's {{cVac}} km/s: m₀/m₁ = {{mrOrb}}.
free.text: Free in space, a rocket and its fuel start at rest together. Each throw of fuel backwards gives the rocket the opposite momentum, and their common centre of mass stays where it was, as Newton showed for any bodies that act only on one another [1]. Since the rocket gets lighter with each throw, each speeds it up more than the last; added up, Δv = u ln(m₀/m₁), with u the exhaust speed relative to the rocket and m₀, m₁ its full and empty masses [2]. A rocket three quarters fuel reaches ln 4 = 1.39 u (1.36 u in 48 separate throws). At {{cVac}} km/s, the 7.9 km/s of a low orbit needs m₀/m₁ = {{mrOrb}}, a rocket {{propOrb}} % fuel before the losses to air and gravity, hence stages. In the animation, 48 throws, each exact: the speed follows Tsiolkovsky's curve, and the last balls, thrown once the rocket goes faster than u, move forward too, more slowly.
free.verdict: Would refute it: a rocket in space whose speed does not follow its mass ratio, or a centre of mass that moves without an outside force.
